questions.topic: What a key does for a row that carries no key of its own
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a surrogate primary key is added
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a table of beekeeper notes has no natural unique column. What does adding an auto-increment id column achieve?

options.text: It gives every row a stable unique identifier
It stores the beekeeper's name as the key
It speeds up all queries automatically
It prevents duplicate rows from being inserted

questions.explanation: A surrogate primary key provides a stable unique identifier for each row regardless of business data. It does not itself prevent duplicates or speed up every query.

questions.topic: Reading a nested document and the query it cannot serve
questions.learningObjective: Identify a query unsupported by nested documents
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a MongoDB document nests an array of tags. Which query cannot be served efficiently without an index on the array field?

options.text: Find documents where tags contains pollen
Find documents where tags array length equals three
Find documents where tags is empty

questions.explanation: Querying by array length requires scanning or a special index, while contains and emptiness checks are better supported. The length condition is the harder one.

questions.topic: A column rename and the query it leaves behind
questions.learningObjective: Recognize stale queries after a rename
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a column is renamed from bee_count to hive_count but an old query still references bee_count. What happens at runtime?

answer.exemplar: The database rejects the query with a column-not-found error because the old name no longer exists after the rename.

questions.explanation: Renaming a column invalidates any query, view, or stored procedure that still uses the old name. Update all references in the same migration.

questions.topic: A backfill run in small batches and the lock it avoids holding
questions.learningObjective: Explain why batched backfills avoid long locks
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a backfill updates a million rows in one transaction. Why is this risky?

options.text: It holds a lock for the entire run

questions.explanation: A single large transaction holds locks and bloats the transaction log. Small batches commit frequently, releasing locks between batches.

questions.topic: A deleted row that a unique index still remembers
questions.learningObjective: Explain soft delete versus unique index
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a soft-deleted row blocks reinserting the same email. Why does the unique index still reject it?

options.text: The row is still physically present

questions.explanation: Soft delete keeps the row in the table, so the unique index still sees the email. A partial unique index excluding deleted rows fixes this.

questions.topic: A unique index that refuses a swap of two values
questions.learningObjective: Explain why swapping unique values fails
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, swapping two rows' unique usernames in one update fails. Why?
questions.explanation: During the update the database checks uniqueness per statement, so the intermediate duplicate violates the constraint. Use a deferred constraint or a temporary value.

questions.topic: A foreign key that refuses an orphan and then a parent
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, inserting a child row with no matching parent fails. What constraint enforces this?

answer.exemplar: The foreign key constraint requires the child's parent reference to match an existing parent row, preventing orphan records.

questions.explanation: Foreign keys enforce referential integrity by rejecting child rows without a matching parent. They also block deleting a parent that still has children.

questions.topic: An index and the plan it replaces
questions.learningObjective: Predict plan change after adding an index
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a query on an unindexed column uses a sequential scan. After adding an index, what changes?

options.text: It still scans because indexes are ignored
It switches to an index scan

questions.explanation: A suitable index lets the planner switch from sequential scan to index scan, reducing rows read. The planner still chooses based on cost.

questions.topic: A composite index and the order its columns have to be in
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a composite index on (a, b) cannot serve a query filtering only on b. Why?

options.text: Composite indexes index all columns equally
The index is sorted by a first
The query needs a full scan always

questions.explanation: A composite index is sorted by the first column then the second, so filtering only on the second column cannot use the index's order. This is the leftmost prefix rule.

questions.topic: A covering index and the table visit it removes
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a query selects columns all present in an index. What table visit is removed?
questions.explanation: A covering index contains all columns needed, so the database skips fetching the heap or table rows. This is an index-only scan.

questions.topic: What a key does for a row that carries no key of its own
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish primary key from unique constraint
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a table has both a primary key and a unique constraint on email. Which one can be null?

options.text: The primary key can be null
The unique constraint column can be null

questions.explanation: Primary keys cannot be null, but unique constraints often allow one or more nulls depending on the database. Nulls are not equal to each other.

questions.topic: Reading a nested document and the query it cannot serve
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a nested document duplicates a user's name in every order. What risk does this create?

answer.exemplar: Updating the user's name requires updating every order document, risking stale data if any update is missed.

questions.explanation: Denormalization speeds reads but complicates writes. Keeping duplicated data consistent requires updating all copies or accepting eventual consistency.

questions.topic: A column rename and the query it leaves behind
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, what is the safest order to rename a column without breaking running queries?

options.text: Add new column, backfill, switch reads, drop old

questions.explanation: The expand-contract pattern adds the new column, backfills it, switches readers, then drops the old one, avoiding downtime. Renaming in place breaks in-flight queries.

questions.topic: A backfill run in small batches and the lock it avoids holding
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how should a backfill batch size be chosen?

options.text: As large as possible to finish fast
Small enough to keep each transaction short

questions.explanation: Batches should be small enough to keep transactions and locks short while still making progress. One row per batch is wastefully slow.

questions.topic: A deleted row that a unique index still remembers
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how do you allow reinserting an email after soft delete?

options.text: Store emails in a separate table
Use a partial unique index excluding deleted rows

questions.explanation: A partial unique index that excludes soft-deleted rows preserves uniqueness for active rows while allowing reuse after deletion. Dropping the index removes protection.

questions.topic: A unique index that refuses a swap of two values
questions.learningObjective: Implement a safe swap of unique values
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how can two rows swap unique usernames without violating the constraint?

answer.exemplar: Update one row to a temporary placeholder value, then update the second, then set the first to the final value, or use a deferred constraint.

questions.explanation: A temporary value or a deferred constraint avoids the intermediate duplicate. Deferred constraints check only at commit time.
questions.hint: Use a temp value or deferred check.

questions.topic: A foreign key that refuses an orphan and then a parent
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, deleting a parent with children fails. Which option removes children automatically?

options.text: ON DELETE SET NULL keeps children
ON DELETE NO ACTION does nothing

questions.explanation: ON DELETE CASCADE deletes child rows when the parent is deleted. RESTRICT blocks, SET NULL nullifies, and NO ACTION defers the check.

questions.topic: An index and the plan it replaces
questions.learningObjective: Identify when an index is not used
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, an index exists but the planner still scans. When does this happen?

options.text: When the index is always used
When the query selects most rows

questions.explanation: If a query returns a large fraction of rows, sequential scan is cheaper than index lookup plus heap fetches. The planner chooses based on estimated cost.

questions.topic: A composite index and the order its columns have to be in
questions.learningObjective: Design a composite index for a query
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a query filters on status then sorts by created_at. Which composite index order is best?
questions.explanation: Put the equality filter column first, then the sort column, so the index both filters and returns rows in order. Reversing loses the filter prefix.

questions.topic: A covering index and the table visit it removes
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how do you make an index cover a query selecting user_id and created_at?

answer.exemplar: Include both selected columns in the index, for example CREATE INDEX idx ON orders(user_id, created_at), so no table fetch is needed.

questions.explanation: A covering index contains every column the query needs. Include selected and filtered columns, keeping index size reasonable.

questions.topic: What a key does for a row that carries no key of its own
questions.learningObjective: Explain natural versus surrogate key choice
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, when is a natural key preferable to a surrogate key?

options.text: When the natural value is stable and meaningful
When the natural value changes often

questions.explanation: A natural key is fine when the business value is stable and unique, like an ISO country code. Surrogates are safer when natural values change or are large.

questions.topic: Reading a nested document and the query it cannot serve
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a query asks for documents where a nested array contains all of three values. What makes it hard?

options.text: It is a simple equality query
It needs no index at all
It requires matching all values in one array

questions.explanation: Matching all specified values within the same nested array requires array intersection logic, which is more complex than single-value containment. Index support varies.

questions.topic: A column rename and the query it leaves behind
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a view references a renamed column. What symptom appears?

options.text: The view returns stale cached data
The view auto-updates to new name
The view fails to compile or query

questions.explanation: Views are stored SQL definitions, so a renamed column breaks them until redefined. Recompile or recreate affected views during migration.

questions.topic: A backfill run in small batches and the lock it avoids holding
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why add a short sleep between backfill batches?

answer.exemplar: The sleep lets other transactions acquire locks and keeps the database responsive during the long backfill.

questions.explanation: Pausing between batches reduces lock contention and gives the database time to process other work. It trades total runtime for availability.

questions.topic: A deleted row that a unique index still remembers
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, which delete keeps the row in the table?

options.text: Soft delete marks the row deleted

questions.explanation: Soft delete sets a deleted flag instead of removing the row, preserving history and auditability. Hard delete physically removes it.

questions.topic: A unique index that refuses a swap of two values
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a deferred unique constraint helps a swap because it checks uniqueness when?
questions.explanation: Deferred constraints are checked at commit time, allowing intermediate duplicates within the transaction. Immediate constraints fail mid-statement.

questions.topic: A foreign key that refuses an orphan and then a parent
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, ON DELETE SET NULL on a child foreign key does what when the parent is deleted?

options.text: Keeps the child referencing a missing parent
Sets the child's foreign key to null

questions.explanation: SET NULL nullifies the child's foreign key column, leaving the child row but removing the reference. It requires the column to be nullable.

questions.topic: An index and the plan it replaces
questions.learningObjective: Compare index scan versus bitmap scan
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, when does a bitmap index scan appear instead of a plain index scan?

answer.exemplar: A bitmap scan appears when many rows match and the planner batches heap fetches to reduce random I/O.

questions.explanation: Bitmap scans collect matching row locations then fetch heap pages in order, improving I/O when many rows match. Plain index scans fetch rows one at a time.

questions.topic: A composite index and the order its columns have to be in
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a composite index on (a, b) with a range filter on a and equality on b uses the index how?

options.text: Uses a for range, b is not used for filtering

questions.explanation: A range condition on the first column stops the leftmost prefix from reaching the second column for filtering. The index still helps on a.

questions.topic: A covering index and the table visit it removes
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, an index-only scan still needs what to avoid visiting the table?

options.text: No columns need to be in the index
All columns must be in the index

questions.explanation: An index-only scan requires every column referenced to be in the index. Missing columns force a heap fetch. Visibility map also matters in some engines.

questions.topic: What a key does for a row that carries no key of its own
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a junction table uses a composite primary key of (user_id, role_id). Why is this appropriate?

options.text: It uniquely identifies each user-role pair

questions.explanation: A composite primary key enforces that each combination of user and role appears once, which is exactly the constraint a junction table needs.

questions.topic: Reading a nested document and the query it cannot serve
questions.learningObjective: Use dot notation for nested fields
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how do you query a nested field address.city in MongoDB?

options.text: Use address.city in the query document

questions.explanation: Dot notation traverses nested fields in MongoDB queries and indexes. Bracket syntax is not used for this purpose.

questions.topic: A column rename and the query it leaves behind
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, after renaming a column, what must be updated besides the database?

answer.exemplar: All application queries, ORM mappings, views, stored procedures, and reports that reference the old column name must be updated.

questions.explanation: A rename touches every layer that uses the column name. Search codebases and database objects for the old name before deploying.

questions.topic: A backfill run in small batches and the lock it avoids holding
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how should a backfill resume after interruption?

options.text: Resume from the last committed batch

questions.explanation: Storing the last processed id or batch marker lets the job resume without reprocessing. Restarting from the beginning wastes work and time.

questions.topic: A deleted row that a unique index still remembers
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, which partial index predicate allows reuse of an email after soft delete?
questions.explanation: Indexing only rows where deleted_at is null enforces uniqueness among active rows while ignoring soft-deleted ones. The opposite predicate would enforce uniqueness among deleted rows.

questions.topic: A unique index that refuses a swap of two values
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why does using a temporary placeholder value allow a swap?
questions.explanation: A placeholder ensures no two rows share the same value at any point, satisfying the unique constraint throughout. The index stays active.

questions.topic: A foreign key that refuses an orphan and then a parent
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, what is the difference between ON DELETE RESTRICT and ON DELETE NO ACTION?

answer.exemplar: RESTRICT checks immediately and blocks deletion, while NO ACTION defers the check to the end of the statement or transaction.

questions.explanation: Both prevent orphan rows, but RESTRICT is immediate and NO ACTION can be deferred. In practice they often behave identically for simple statements.

questions.topic: An index and the plan it replaces
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, which EXPLAIN node indicates a full table read?
questions.explanation: Seq Scan means the database reads every row of the table. Index Scan, Nested Loop, and Sort describe other operations.

questions.topic: A composite index and the order its columns have to be in
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, for a query filtering on a and b with equality on both, which index column order is acceptable?
questions.explanation: With equality on both columns, either order can serve the query because both are prefix-usable. Range or sort conditions would make order matter.

questions.topic: A covering index and the table visit it removes
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why might a covering index be a bad idea for a large table?

options.text: It speeds up all queries for free
It slows down writes and uses more storage

questions.explanation: Covering indexes duplicate columns, increasing storage and write overhead. They help only queries that need those columns.

questions.topic: What a key does for a row that carries no key of its own
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why is a stable primary key valuable for foreign key relationships?

answer.exemplar: A stable primary key never changes, so foreign keys referencing it remain valid and joins stay consistent over time.

questions.explanation: If a primary key changes, all foreign key references must update or break. Surrogate keys avoid this by staying constant.

questions.topic: Reading a nested document and the query it cannot serve
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how do you index a nested array field tags in MongoDB?

options.text: Create a multikey index on tags

questions.explanation: A multikey index creates an index entry for each array element, enabling efficient containment queries on nested arrays.

questions.topic: A column rename and the query it leaves behind
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how can a rename be made backward compatible temporarily?

options.text: Create a view with the old column name

questions.explanation: A view exposing the old column name lets old code keep working while new code uses the renamed column. Remove the view after migration completes.

questions.topic: A backfill run in small batches and the lock it avoids holding
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why should backfill updates be idempotent?

options.text: So re-running a batch is safe
So the table can be dropped

questions.explanation: Idempotent updates let a retried or resumed batch produce the same result without corrupting data. This is essential for safe retries after failures.

questions.topic: A deleted row that a unique index still remembers
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why must queries exclude soft-deleted rows?

answer.exemplar: Otherwise deleted records appear in results, violating user expectations and breaking uniqueness assumptions.

questions.explanation: Soft-deleted rows remain in the table, so every read must filter them out. Forgetting this leaks deleted data into results.

questions.topic: A unique index that refuses a swap of two values
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, when is an immediate unique constraint checked?
questions.explanation: Immediate constraints are validated as each statement runs, rejecting violations at that point. Deferred constraints wait until commit.

questions.topic: A foreign key that refuses an orphan and then a parent
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, adding a foreign key to a large table with existing bad data fails. What is the safest approach?

options.text: Add it NOT VALID then validate later

questions.explanation: Adding the constraint as NOT VALID avoids scanning all rows immediately, then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT checks existing data later without locking writes as long.

questions.topic: An index and the plan it replaces
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, after a large data load the planner chooses bad plans. What maintenance fixes this?
questions.explanation: ANALYZE updates table statistics so the planner estimates row counts and selectivity correctly. Stale statistics lead to poor plan choices.

questions.topic: A composite index and the order its columns have to be in
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why does putting the ORDER BY column first in an index sometimes avoid a sort?

answer.exemplar: If the index is ordered by the same column as ORDER BY, the database can return rows already in that order without an explicit sort step.

questions.explanation: Matching index order to ORDER BY lets the planner skip the sort operation. Equality filters should still precede the sort column when possible.

questions.topic: A covering index and the table visit it removes
questions.learningObjective: Identify when covering is not possible
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why can SELECT * rarely use an index-only scan?

options.text: It requests columns not in the index

questions.explanation: SELECT * requests all columns, but an index rarely contains all of them, forcing a heap fetch. Selecting only needed columns enables covering.

questions.topic: What a key does for a row that carries no key of its own
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why are big surrogate keys like UUIDs costly for indexes?

options.text: They are always faster to generate
They make index entries larger and slower

questions.explanation: Large keys widen index entries, consuming more memory and I/O. Sequential integer keys are more cache-friendly than random UUIDs.

questions.topic: Reading a nested document and the query it cannot serve
questions.learningObjective: Explain when to embed versus reference
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, when should a related entity be referenced rather than embedded?

options.text: When the related entity is large or shared by many

questions.explanation: Embedding suits small, owned, frequently read data. Referencing suits large or shared entities to avoid duplication and unbounded document growth.

questions.topic: A column rename and the query it leaves behind
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, before renaming a column, which dependency is easiest to miss?
questions.explanation: External services and other repositories may reference the column through APIs or raw queries, and are easy to overlook. Audit all consumers before renaming.

questions.topic: A backfill run in small batches and the lock it avoids holding
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why can a backfill still cause lock contention even in small batches?

answer.exemplar: Each batch still takes row or table locks while updating, and frequent commits create checkpoint pressure.

questions.explanation: Small batches reduce but do not eliminate locking. Concurrent writers may wait on locks held by each batch, and many commits increase I/O pressure.

questions.topic: A deleted row that a unique index still remembers
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, instead of soft delete, what alternative preserves uniqueness and history?

options.text: Keep all rows with a flag
Move deleted rows to an archive table

questions.explanation: An archive table moves deleted rows out of the main table, preserving history while keeping the main table's unique index clean. Soft delete keeps them in place.

questions.topic: A unique index that refuses a swap of two values
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, how can a single UPDATE swap two unique values safely?

options.text: Use a CASE expression mapping both values at once
Use a transaction with no commit

questions.explanation: A single UPDATE with CASE assigns both new values in one statement, but uniqueness is still checked per row; some engines still reject. Deferred constraints are more reliable.

questions.topic: A foreign key that refuses an orphan and then a parent
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, why should foreign key columns be indexed?

options.text: Indexing is never needed for foreign keys
To speed up joins and parent lookups

questions.explanation: Indexing foreign key columns speeds up joins and the checks performed when deleting or updating parent rows. Some databases do not auto-create these indexes.

questions.topic: An index and the plan it replaces
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, what causes an index to become bloated and slow?

answer.exemplar: Frequent updates and deletes leave dead entries in the index, increasing its size and slowing scans until it is rebuilt or vacuumed.

questions.explanation: Bloat comes from dead tuples and page splits. Regular vacuuming or reindexing reclaims space and restores performance.

questions.topic: A composite index and the order its columns have to be in
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, a query filters on a and selects b. What composite index order is optimal?
questions.explanation: The filter column a comes first for prefix matching, and b follows to cover the selected column. Reversing loses the filter prefix.

questions.topic: A covering index and the table visit it removes
questions.stem: In fixing a common mistake, what metric best shows an index-only scan helped?

options.text: Reduced heap fetches or buffer reads

questions.explanation: Fewer heap fetches and buffer reads indicate the index satisfied the query without table visits. Writes and scan counts are not the right signals.
